title: Functions & Scope
blurb: Signatures, packing and unpacking, closures: design functions that state exactly what shape of input they accept and remember what they need to.

cells.title: The signature is a contract
cells.body:
A function's signature tells every caller — including future you — what shapes of input it accepts and what it hands back. Python lets the contract be flexible: *args collects any extra positional arguments into a tuple, and **kwargs collects any extra keyword arguments into a dict. That means a function can honestly say 'give me at least one reading, then as many more as you have' instead of forcing callers to wrap everything in a list by hand.

The discipline that separates clean code from spaghetti: a function should return its answer, not print it; every parameter should have a default or a reason not to; and the moment you write a function that takes four booleans, redesign the signature (flags-as-parameters is a design smell). Reasoning about a call is only possible when the contract is small and sharp.

cells.title: Packing at the definition, unpacking at the call
cells.body:
The * and ** symbols do two mirrored jobs. In a definition they pack many incoming values into one tuple/dict. In a call they unpack: f(*parts) feeds each element of parts as its own argument, and {**a, **b} splats two dicts into a new one — where keys in b win because it is unpacked later. Precedence from unpacking order is a precise, mechanical rule: the rightmost source for a key decides its value.

This one construct is the idiomatic answer to a whole family of 'merge these settings' problems. Note what it does NOT do: it replaces values wholesale — a dict from the right completely replaces a dict from the left, there is no recursive merging unless you write it. Knowing exactly where the built-in behavior stops is what lets you reach for it with confidence.

cells.title: Closures: functions that carry their own state
cells.body:
When you return a function from a function, the inner function keeps a live reference to the variables of the function that built it. That bundle — the code plus the captured environment — is a closure. Each call of the outer factory creates a fresh set of captured variables, so two counters built by the same factory count independently: this is object-like state without writing a class.

To modify a captured variable (not just read it), the inner function must declare nonlocal; otherwise assignment silently creates a new local and the captured value goes untouched — a classic bug. Closures power decorators, callback registration, and partial application, so being able to reason about 'which variable cell does this function object refer to?' is a core fluency.

demo.code:
def make_meter(start):
    reading = start
    def meter():
        nonlocal reading
        reading += 1
        return reading
    return meter

m1, m2 = make_meter(10), make_meter(0)
print(m1(), m1(), m2(), m1())  # two independent meters

exercise.title: Weigh Station Bounds
exercise.statement:
A weigh station checks a truck whose crates arrive one at a time, so the scale reports each crate weight as its own argument — the station cannot know in advance how many crates a truck carries. Some crates contain buoyant foam and register negative weights.

Write load_bounds(*weights) that accepts any number of integer weights and returns a tuple (lightest, heaviest). A truck with no crates at all yields (0, 0). Use the varargs signature — the whole point is not forcing callers to build a list.
constraints: each weight is an integer between -500 and 500
a single argument means lightest == heaviest

examples.why: the smallest reading is 3, the largest is 9
foam crates pull the lightest bound below zero

exercise.starter:
def load_bounds(*weights):
    """Return (lightest, heaviest) of the given weights.

    No arguments at all -> (0, 0).
    """
    pass
hints: What does the * in *weights already do for you — what kind of value is weights inside the function body?
weights arrives as a tuple. The empty case is the only special one; after guarding it, built-ins do the aggregation.
if not weights: return (0, 0) — otherwise return (min(weights), max(weights)). Remember to return a tuple, not two separate values.
exercise.reasoning: The varargs signature moves a structural decision into the function: callers never package the data, so there is no 'do I pass a list or spread it?' confusion at every call site. Inside, weights is just a tuple, so aggregation functions that accept any iterable apply directly. The one branch worth writing deliberately is the empty input: min() of nothing raises ValueError, so the contract '(0, 0) for an empty truck' has to be handled before any aggregation runs. Deciding empty-input behavior up front — and putting it in the docstring — is what makes a varargs contract trustworthy.

exercise.title: Layered Release Settings
exercise.statement:
A deployment tool resolves configuration in layers: a base dict, then a sequence of override layers from a config file, a CI job, and finally a command line. A key set in a later layer always wins over the same key in an earlier layer; layers may also introduce keys the base never had. A value that is itself a dict is replaced wholesale — there is no deep merging.

Implement merge_config(base, *patches) returning the resolved dict as a new dict (never mutate the inputs). Later patches override earlier ones and the base.
constraints: base and every patch is a dict with string keys
values may be ints, strings, lists or nested dicts; a patch value always replaces the previous value entirely

examples.why: the patch overrides retries but mode survives from the base
the last layer to mention a key decides it; new keys accumulate

exercise.starter:
def merge_config(base, *patches):
    """Resolve layered config dicts into one new dict.

    base is the foundation; each patch (in order) overrides keys it
    mentions and adds keys it introduces. Inputs are never mutated.
    """
    pass
hints: If you merged exactly two dicts in one expression, which one would win? How does that extend when you fold in a third?
Start from a copy of base, then fold each patch in, in order. dict.update (or {**merged, **patch}) applied left to right gives later layers the final say.
merged = dict(base); for patch in patches: merged.update(patch); return merged. Making a copy first is what guarantees the inputs are untouched.
exercise.reasoning: Precedence is nothing more than order of application: if you fold layers left to right and each fold lets the incoming dict overwrite existing keys, then 'later wins' is automatic — you never need an explicit rule about precedence because the fold encodes it. Two correctness details make the function production-grade: starting from dict(base) (a copy) so inputs are never mutated, and documenting that nested dicts are replaced rather than deep-merged, which is exactly what update does. When you genuinely need a deep merge, that is a recursive function you write on purpose — knowing where the shallow default ends is the point.
exercise.solution:
def merge_config(base, *patches):
    merged = dict(base)          # copy: never touch the caller's dicts
    for patch in patches:        # later layers overwrite earlier ones
        merged.update(patch)
    return merged

exercise.title: Two Turnstiles
exercise.statement:
A venue gate has two turnstiles, A and B, each with its own clicker. A clicker is made by make_counter(start): it returns a zero-argument callable whose first call returns start, second call start + 1, and so on — each turnstile remembers its own clicks, independent of the other.

Implement make_counter(start) and the driver interleaved_trace(start_a, start_b, script). The script is a list of the tags "a" and "b"; the driver builds one counter per turnstile from the given starts and returns the list of counter outputs in script order. If your two counters accidentally share state, the interleaved output exposes it immediately.
constraints: script contains only the tags 'a' and 'b'
start values are integers between -1000 and 1000

examples.why: counter A emits 0 then 1; counter B emits 100 — each keeps its own place
two clicks of turnstile A only

exercise.starter:
def make_counter(start):
    """Return a zero-arg callable counting start, start+1, start+2, ...

    Every call of make_counter produces an INDEPENDENT counter.
    """
    pass


def interleaved_trace(start_a, start_b, script):
    """Click turnstile counters A and B per the script tags.

    Build counter_a from start_a and counter_b from start_b, then for
    each tag in script append that counter's next value. Return the
    list of values in order.
    """
    pass
hints: Where must the 'current value' live so that two counters built by the same factory do not see each other's clicks?
The state lives in a variable of make_counter itself, captured by the inner function. Declare nonlocal to update it, and remember to return the value BEFORE advancing (the first call returns start).
value = start; def counter(): nonlocal value; result = value; value += 1; return result; return counter. The driver then appends counter_a() or counter_b() per tag.
exercise.reasoning: Each call of make_counter runs the outer function's body again, creating a brand new variable cell that only the returned function can see. That is the entire mechanism behind 'independent counters' — no class, no shared dict, just one closure per factory call. The nonlocal declaration matters because assignment without it would create a fresh local named value inside the inner function, and the captured cell would never advance. The interleaved driver is a state-separation test in disguise: a shared or global counter produces the right values for each turnstile in isolation but the wrong interleaved sequence — which is precisely the class of bug that closures, used correctly, make impossible.
exercise.solution:
def make_counter(start):
    value = start
    def counter():
        nonlocal value
        result = value
        value += 1
        return result
    return counter


def interleaved_trace(start_a, start_b, script):
    counter_a = make_counter(start_a)
    counter_b = make_counter(start_b)
    out = []
    for tag in script:
        out.append(counter_a() if tag == "a" else counter_b())
    return out

exercise.title: Controlled Unpacking
exercise.statement:
A shipping manifest represents cargo as nested lists: a crate contains parts and sub-crates, sub-crates may contain more sub-crates, and so on. The dock crew can only open depth levels of packaging per order — anything nested deeper than that stays inside its box.

Implement flatten_nested(items, depth): expand list nesting up to depth levels; lists still nested deeper than the budget remain intact as list values. Only lists count as packaging — tuples and strings are ordinary parts. An empty list holds nothing, so opening it contributes no elements. A budget of 0 opens nothing (but still returns a fresh list).
constraints: items contains ints, strings and lists; only lists are packaging
0 <= depth <= 10 and nesting never exceeds 10 levels
the result must be a NEW list even when nothing is expanded

examples.why: two levels of packaging open; the list around 4 is three deep and stays sealed
a zero budget opens nothing at all

exercise.starter:
def flatten_nested(items, depth):
    """Expand nested lists up to depth levels of packaging.

    Lists nested deeper than depth stay intact as values. Only lists
    count as packaging; depth 0 returns the items unchanged (as a new
    list).
    """
    pass
hints: If you open one level of packaging, what is the remaining budget for the contents that were inside it? What does a budget of 0 tell you to do?

Recurse: for each item, if it is a list and the budget is positive, splice in flatten_nested(item, depth - 1); otherwise keep the item as-is. The base case is depth == 0 — return a copy with nothing opened.

if depth <= 0: return list(items). Then loop: out = []; for item in items: out.extend(flatten_nested(item, depth - 1)) if it is a list, else out.append(item). Note isinstance(item, list) — tuples must not match.
exercise.reasoning: The recursion is driven by one number: the remaining budget. Each level of the recursion answers the same question at a smaller scale — 'open up to k levels of what I was given' — and the list case answers it by delegating with depth - 1. The base case is not 'empty list' but 'zero budget', and getting that choice right is the whole exercise: an empty list and a budget of zero are different situations, and the sealed-lists-deeper-down requirement falls out of the budget running out, not of any special-case check. Guarding the recursion with isinstance(item, list) (never a looser check) is what keeps tuples and strings sealed — a detail that quietly tests whether you know which types your code actually matches.
